roles: halakhist (posek) and codifier of Jewish law
summary: Joseph Karo (1488-1575) was the preeminent halakhic codifier of the early modern period, active in Ottoman Safed, author of the Beit Yosef, a vast commentary on Jacob ben Asher's Tur, and of the Shulchan Aruch ('The Set Table', first printed Venice 1565), which with the Ashkenazi glosses of Moses Isserles (the Mappah) came to be regarded across much of the Jewish world as the authoritative code of Jewish law. He was also a kabbalist whose mystical diary, the Maggid Meisharim, records what it presents as revelations from a maggid, a heavenly mentor identified in the diary with the personified Mishnah.
description:
Joseph Karo, born in 1488 into the generation of the Iberian expulsions (his family left the Iberian Peninsula in his childhood, in the wake of the 1492 expulsion of the Jews from Spain), lived in the Ottoman lands and settled in Safed (Tzfat) in the Galilee, then a gathering point for Sephardic exiles and a centre of kabbalistic activity. He is recorded in the tradition as the leading halakhic authority of his age and as a member of the mystical circle of Safed. He died in Safed in 1575.

Karo's principal legal works are two linked projects. The first is the Beit Yosef ('House of Joseph'), a vast commentary built on the Arba'ah Turim (the 'Tur') of Jacob ben Asher, in which Karo traces each law back through the Talmud and the later authorities and argues his rulings; the tradition treats it as one of the great works of halakhic analysis. Out of it he distilled the Shulchan Aruch ('The Set Table'), a concise digest of practical law arranged in four parts following the structure of the Tur (Orach Chayim, Yoreh De'ah, Even ha-Ezer, Choshen Mishpat), first printed in Venice in 1565. Its opening ruling, at Orach Chayim 1:1, reads: 'One should strengthen himself like a lion to get up in the morning to serve his creator.' Karo's method in resolving disputed law is generally described as following the majority among three earlier authorities, Isaac Alfasi (the Rif), Maimonides (the Rambam), and Asher ben Jehiel (the Rosh). Because this method reflected largely Sephardic precedent, the Ashkenazi authority Moses Isserles of Krakow (the Rema) added glosses recording Ashkenazi custom and ruling where it diverged, a layer he called the Mappah ('the Tablecloth') spread over Karo's 'Set Table'; the two together, printed on the same page, came to be regarded within the tradition as the authoritative code of Jewish law across both Sephardic and Ashkenazi communities. This entry states that standing as the tradition's own regard for the work, not as a ruling of the editor. The first printing already interwove a further voice, since the very opening gloss at Orach Chayim 1:1 is Isserles' Hagah, which cites 'I have set the Lord always before me' (Psalm 16:8) as 'a great principle in the Torah', drawing on Maimonides' Guide for the Perplexed III:52.

Alongside the codifier stands the mystic. Karo kept a mystical diary, published as the Maggid Meisharim ('Preacher of Righteousness'), which records over decades what the diary presents as nocturnal visitations and speeches of a maggid, a heavenly mentor or 'preacher' that the text identifies with the personified Mishnah and with the Shekhinah, addressing Karo, admonishing him in matters of ascetic practice and study, and promising him spiritual attainments. The diary is written largely as the speech of the maggid to Karo in the first person. This entry presents these revelations as what the diary reports and as what the tradition transmits under Karo's name, not as events the editor affirms or denies. The standard modern study, R. J. Zwi Werblowsky's Joseph Karo: Lawyer and Mystic, takes as its explicit problem the union in one person of the sober legal codifier and the visionary diarist, and argues that in the setting of sixteenth-century Safed the two roles were not felt as a contradiction; contemporary scholarship (Roni Weinstein) situates Karo's codification project within the early modern Ottoman and wider Eurasian legal world and reads his law and his mysticism as parts of a single enterprise.

Karo belonged to the Safed circle, the concentration of kabbalists and halakhists in the Galilean town in the sixteenth century that included Solomon Alkabetz and Moses Cordovero and, in the following generation, Isaac Luria. His code was later reworked from within Hasidism by Shneur Zalman of Liady, whose Shulchan Aruch ha-Rav recast Karo's rulings with their reasons. This entry records Karo on the tradition's own terms as author of the Beit Yosef and the Shulchan Aruch and as the diarist of the Maggid Meisharim, with the work's authoritative standing and the diary's revelations attributed to the tradition and to Karo's own text rather than asserted by the editor.

Died in Safed in 1575.

Isaac Luria (the Arizal), of the following generation at Safed, is recorded in the tradition as having been present at Karo's circle; the two are linked as members of the Safed kabbalistic milieu (Luria arriving toward the end of Karo's life).
